results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You’ll need to keep tax‑related records for a period that depends on the type of record and any period‑of‑limitations rule that applies to the tax year.  Headlines from IRS Publication 583 (Starting a Business) are:

* **All tax‑return records** – Keep any records that support an item of income or deduction on a return **for the period of limitations for that return** (the time the IRS can assess additional tax or you can amend the return).  The publication states:  
  “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code. Generally, this means you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **Employment‑tax records** – If you have employees, the rule is a fixed 4‑year period:  
  “You must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **Asset/property records** – Keep any records related to the purchase, use, or sale of property **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **Other records** – Once records are no longer needed for tax purposes, you may keep them longer if required for other reasons (e.g., insurance, creditors) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

In short, the documents require you to retain tax records for the time the IRS can claim or you can amend, or for a fixed 4 years for employment taxes, and for asset records until the limitations period for the final disposition year expires.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several reasons that the IRS documents state explicitly:

* **To monitor the progress of your business** – good records let you see whether your business is improving, which items are selling, or what changes you need to make.  
  [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)]

* **To prepare accurate financial statements** – the figures in your records are what you use to produce income (profit‑and‑loss) statements and balance sheets, which help you deal with banks or creditors and manage the business.  
  [cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)]

* **To support the entries in your books and on your tax return** – supporting documents such as receipts, invoices, deposit slips, and canceled checks back up every item you report, so the IRS can verify that your income, expenses, and credits are correct.  
  [cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)]

* **To keep them available for IRS inspection** – the IRS can examine your tax returns at any time, so having complete records speeds the examination and lets you explain the items reported.  
  [cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)]

* **To satisfy federal record‑keeping requirements** – the IRS requires you to keep records that support items of income or deduction for as long as the applicable period of limitations runs out, and for employment‑tax records at least four years after they are due or paid.  
  [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)]



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 11)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
The documents explain the basic choices and the situations that guide them.  

**1. Cash method** – report income when you receive it and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them.  
• You can use the cash method “if you keep no inventory” or if you are a “small business taxpayer” that treats inventories as non‑incidental materials or supplies.  
• It is “easier to keep records” for individuals and sole proprietors with no inventory.  
[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)]

**2. Accrual method** – report income in the year it is earned, whether or not payment is received, and deduct or capitalize expenses when they are incurred.  
• If you must keep an inventory (e.g., you produce, purchase, or sell merchandise), you “must generally use an accrual method of accounting for purchases and sales.”  
• Even as a small business, if inventory is necessary, the accrual method is required.  
[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)]  
[cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)]

**3. Special or combination methods** – you can use a mix of cash, accrual, and special methods, but the mix must “clearly show your income” and be consistent.  
• If inventory is required, you must use an accrual method for purchases and sales; the cash method may be used for other items.  
• When you choose a combination, you treat it as the cash method if it includes the cash method.  
[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)]

**4. Choosing the method** – you pick an accounting method when you file your first business income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040).  
• If you have never filed a business return, you can adopt either the calendar‑tax year with the cash method or a fiscal tax year with the accrual method, subject to inventory rules.  
• “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method” – unless you qualify as a small business taxpayer that can treat inventories as non‑incidental materials or supplies.  
[cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)]  
[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)]

**Bottom line:**  
* Use the **cash method** if you have no inventory (or qualify as a small business that treats inventories as non‑incidental materials or supplies).  
* Use the **accrual method** if you keep an inventory or if the cash method would not “clearly reflect income.”  
* If you need or want to mix methods, do so only in a way that still “clearly shows your income” and complies with the rules on inventory and combination methods.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)
3. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To spot and control hazards in your workplace, follow the OSHA Small‑Business Safety and Health Handbook’s **self‑inspection** process:

1. **Conduct routine self‑inspections**  
   *Use knowledgeable, experienced workers to examine your work processes directly.*  
   “An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i.e., self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.”  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

2. **Identify, control, and monitor hazards** – the three core goals of each inspection.  
   * “Small business employers should conduct routine workplace self‑inspections to:  
   • identify hazards,  
   • control identified hazards, and  
   • monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.”  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

3. **Use the hand‑book’s self‑inspection checklists** as a starting point.  
   * The checklists are meant for general‑industry workplaces (not construction or maritime) and give a practical way to begin finding and addressing hazards.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

4. **Compile and review the data**.  
   * Combine checklist results with injury/illness records, training logs, maintenance logs, and incident reports to see where hazards persist or new ones arise.  
   [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

5. **Take action and keep records**.  
   * Once a hazard is identified, implement a control (engineering, administrative, or PPE), train workers, and re‑inspect to confirm the control is effective.  

6. **Make the process part of your safety program**.  
   * OSHA’s recommended practices view hazard identification and control as a systematic element of a safety & health program, and regular inspections are an important tool for that purpose.  
   [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)  

By following these steps—regular self‑inspections, using the book’s checklists, documenting findings, and actively managing controls—you can systematically check your workplace for hazards and keep them under control.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 8)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 7)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash vs. accrual accounting** | Feature | Cash method | Accrual method | |---------|-------------|----------------| | **When income is counted** | When it is actually received (or constructively received) | When it is earned, even if payment comes later | | **When expenses are counted** | When the expense is actually paid (or constructively paid) | When the expense is incurred, regardless of when it is paid | | **Typical use** | • Small businesses with little or no inventory
• Businesses that want a simpler record‑keeping system | • Businesses that sell products or services on credit
• Business that need to match income and expenses in the same tax year | **Citations** - *IRS Publication 583 – Starting a Business* (page 5) “1. Cash method. Under the cash method, you report income in the tax year you receive it. You usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you pay them. 2. Accrual method. Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it, even though you may receive payment in a later year. You deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you incur them, whether or not you pay them that year.” [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)] - *IRS Publication 334 – Tax Guide for Small Business* (page 15) “Under the cash method, you generally deduct expenses in the tax year in which you actually pay them.” [cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)] - *IRS Publication 334 – Tax Guide for Small Business* (page 16) “Under an accrual method of accounting, you generally report income in the year earned and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year incurred.” [cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)] These excerpts show the core difference: cash accounting records when money changes hands, while accrual accounting records when transactions are earned or incurred. **Sources:** 1. results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
You may deduct the ordinary and necessary expenses of traveling away from home for your business, such as transportation, lodging, meals, and certain incidental costs.  
- The cost of a car, airplane, train, bus, or other travel between your home and the business destination is deductible.  
- Meals and lodging are deductible only on overnight or “long‑enough” trips that require sleep or rest; you can deduct the actual expenses or use the standard meal allowance, and usually only 50 % of meal costs are allowed.  
- Other deductible items include dry cleaning while traveling, business‑related telephone calls, and tips paid for services.  
- Reimbursements you give to employees for travel and meal expenses are generally deductible, depending on whether the reimbursement plan is accountable or non‑accountable.  

These rules are all set out in IRS Publication 334 (Tax Guide for Small Business)【irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 41】.

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
The SBA’s Business Planning Guide says the executive summary should be a **brief, one‑ or two‑paragraph overview of what you want to accomplish**. It should include:

- **Your business idea**  
- **How much money you need and what you need it for**  
- **How much money you will bring (or have already invested)**  
- **A brief schedule of your goals**  

The section advises writing this part last, after the rest of the plan is complete.  

> “This portion should be brief; usually one or two paragraphs, but it should give the reader an overview of what you want to accomplish. For example, describe your idea, how much money you need, what you need it for, how much money you will bring (or have put) into the business, and a brief schedule of your goals. Since you won’t know some of these facts until you complete your business plan, write this section last.”  
>  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)



**Sources:**
1. [sba_business_planning_guide.pdf (Page 4)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market, you should:

- Identify your market niche and specify who your “best customer” is.  
- Describe the characteristics of those customers.  For business markets these can be industry, company size, location, or product use/application; for consumer markets you can use demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
- Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales‑tax data, industry information, etc., and estimate how much of the total market you expect to capture.  

[sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 14]

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
The ADA Guide for Small Businesses shows that a retail shop *must* provide accessible facilities when doing so is *readily achievable*. The key points are: | Requirement | What the guide says | |-------------|---------------------| | **Accessible entrance** | “Providing physical access to a facility … having only one step at the entrance can prevent access by a person using a wheelchair… If a business has two public entrances, in most cases, only one must be accessible.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) | | **Ramp/step removal** | “When a ramp is added to provide an accessible entrance, the slope of the ramp should be as shallow as possible but **not more than 1:12**.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) | | **Accessible parking** | “Designated accessible parking spaces must be provided **if doing so is readily achievable**.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)
“If the parking lot has 25 or fewer spaces, then 1 must be an accessible parking space. If it has 50 or fewer spaces, it should have 2.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9) | | **Counter and aisle width** | “An accessible sales counter at a cash register … must be **at least 36 inches long** and **no more than 36 inches above the floor**. A space **at least 30 inches by 48 inches** in front of the counter is required.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) | | **Accessible route through the store** | “A 36‑inch‑wide accessible route is needed between displays and shelves… If an accessible route is not provided to all sales areas, alternative services such as staff‑assisted retrieval **must be provided**.” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) | **Bottom line** - If you can reasonably add an accessible entrance (or modify an existing one with a ramp of slope 1:12, handrails, and a wide landing), you must do so. - Add the minimum number of accessible parking spaces described above, and make them reachable via an accessible route from the parking lot to the entrance. - Make at least one counter (or an auxiliary counter) available at 36 inches high, with a clear 30×48‑inch space in front. - Keep all aisles at least 36 inches wide, and provide staff assistance for any areas that cannot be made fully accessible. If a barrier is *not readily achievable*, the guide allows a waiver, but you must document why it is impractical and offer alternative services. (for example, a short ramp that would violate the 1:12 slope). Thus, unless you can prove that making these changes is not readily achievable, the document requires your shop to be wheelchair accessible. **Sources:** 1. results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You’re partially exempt if you meet **either** of the following conditions (see OSHA 131 Small Business Safety and Health Handbook):

- **10 or fewer workers** during **all of the last calendar year** (29 CFR 1904.1) – you are not required to keep OSHA Form 300, 301, or 300A.  
  [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)]

- **Operated in a low‑hazard industry** listed in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A – the employer is also exempt from keeping the standard injury‑recording forms.  
  [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)]

**What you still must do**

All employers, regardless of size or industry, are required to **report** the following to OSHA:

- Work‑related fatalities
- In‑patient hospitalizations
- Amputations
- Loss of an eye

The reporting deadlines are 8 hours for fatalities and 24 hours for the other events.  
[ cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)]

So, if your business has 10 or fewer workers **or** operates in one of OSHA’s designated low‑hazard industries, you are exempt from keeping the daily injury log (Form 300) and the incident reports (Form 301).  However, you must still report the above severe cases to OSHA by the stated time limits.



**Sources:**
1. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
**1. What records to keep for federal tax purposes**

| Type of record | What to keep | How long to keep it (as per the IRS Publication 583) |
|----------------|--------------|--------------------------------------------|
| **Documentation that supports every item of income or deduction** | Receipts, invoices, cancelled checks, bank deposit slips, etc. | Keep them **as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code**.  In practice, that means you should keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out (the period of time in which you can amend your return to claim a credit or refund, or the IRS can assess additional tax). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Employment‑tax records** | Payroll vouchers, W‑2 and W‑3 copies, unemployment‑tax filings, etc. | Keep **all employment‑tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Asset‑related records** | Purchase invoices, sales contracts, depreciation schedules, cost‑basis documents, etc. | Keep them **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition**. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Filed tax returns** | Copies of each filed Form 1040, Schedule C, 1120, etc. | Keep them **for at least the period of limitations for the return**; they also help prepare future returns or amended returns. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **Other supporting documents** | Any document that could be requested by the IRS to substantiate amounts reported on the return (e.g., vendor invoices, bank statements, etc.). | Maintain them for the same length of time as the records that support the item of income or deduction they verify—generally until the applicable period of limitations ends. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16) |

**2. What records to keep for occupational injuries and illnesses**

| Record | What to keep | Retention period |
|--------|--------------|-----------------|
| **OSHA Form 300 – Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | A monthly log of all work‑related injuries and illnesses, except minor first‑aid events. | Keep for **at least five years** after the injury or illness occurred, or the end of the year in which the injury was logged, whichever is later. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 301 – Injury and Illness Incident Report** | A supplementary detailed report for each recordable incident recorded on Form 300. | Also retained for **at least five years**. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **OSHA Form 300A – Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses** | Annual summary of the year’s injury and illness data, used for reporting to OSHA. | Retained for **five years**. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Work‑site fatality, hospitalization, amputation, or eye‑loss reports** | Any incident requiring a fatality or severe‑injury report to OSHA. | Must be **electronically submitted to OSHA by March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered**; records themselves should also be kept **at least five years**. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Medical and exposure records** | Records of employee medical treatment related to work‑related injuries or illnesses, and records of employee exposure to hazardous substances. | Retain for the **time period required for each specific type of record** (e.g., 3 years for most medical records, longer for records of certain exposures). [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Worker training records** | Records of training required by OSHA standards that are relevant to injury prevention. | Keep them **and make them accessible for review by workers**; retention length is as required by the specific OSHA standard, but generally **at least five years** if they relate to injury/illness prevention. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |

**3. Summary**

*For tax records,* keep supporting documentation for as long as the IRS may need to examine it—typically until the period of limitations for the related return expires, plus at least 4 years for employment‐tax records and until the final disposition of any asset for asset records.  

*For injury/illness records,* OSHA requires five‑year retention of all Forms 300, 301, and 300A, as well as any fatality, hospitalization, amputation, or eye‑loss incidents, and associated medical and exposure records.  

These retention requirements come directly from the cited IRS and OSHA publications.

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep your employees safe and make your premises accessible, you should follow the requirements and recommendations from both the OSHA Small‑Business Safety and Health Handbook and the ADA “Guide for Small Businesses.”

---

### 1. Keep Employees Safe – OSHA Requirements  

| Step | What to do | OSHA handbook reference |
|------|-----------|--------------------------|
| **Create a safety and health program** | Adopt a program built around the seven core elements: management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification and assessment, hazard prevention and control, education and training, program evaluation and improvement, and communication and coordination. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| **Identify and control hazards** | Conduct regular workplace inspections to identify hazards and implement controls that prevent injury or illness. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| **Educate employees** | Provide job‑specific training and general safety education so workers know how to avoid hazards. | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| **Comply with the General Duty Clause** | Furnish an employment place that is free from recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious physical harm. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91) |
| **Use OSHA resources** | Request an On‑Site Consultation or use voluntary programs such as the Outreach Training Program or Voluntary Protection Programs to improve safety. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90) |

---

### 2. Make Your Premises Accessible – ADA Requirements  

| Requirement | What to do | ADA guide reference |
|-------------|------------|---------------------|
| **Accessible entrance(s)** | Install a ramp or other accessible path if the original entrance has steps.  The ramp slope must **not exceed 1:12**; handrails are required whenever the slope is steeper than 1:20 or the rise exceeds 6 inches.  Place a sign to direct customers to the accessible entrance. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Accessible parking** | Provide at least one accessible parking space with an access aisle.  The space, aisle, and route to the building entrance must have firm, slip‑resistant surfaces, no steps or steep slopes, and enough clearance.  Mark spaces with the international symbol of accessibility. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Doors and door hardware** | Use at least a 36‑inch wide opening (32 inches when fully opened).  Replace or modify door handles that require tight grasping (e.g., round knobs or thumb latches) with lever or loop handles.  If a narrow turnstile is used, provide an accessible turnstile, gate, or opening. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Other barriers** | Remove or modify any other architectural barriers that prevent people with disabilities from accessing goods or services, prioritizing entrance accessibility, public toilets, and public‑use areas. | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) |

---

#### Summary
- **Safety:** Build a full safety‑and‑health program, identify hazards, train employees, and meet the General Duty Clause.
- **Accessibility:** Ensure at least one accessible entrance (ramp ≤ 1:12 slope, handrails), provide accessible parking, and make doors and hardware usable for all customers.

Following these documented steps will help you protect employees and make your business welcoming to everyone.

results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**How to write a business plan (based on the SBA Business Planning Guide)**  

1. **Start with a clear outline.**  
   The guide recommends the following core sections:
   * Cover page – company name, address, phone, owners, date, and logo if available.  
   * Executive summary – a brief (one‑to‑two‑paragraph) overview of the plan’s purpose, the amount of money needed, and a high‑level schedule of goals. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
   * Business section – describe the product or service, competitive advantage, regulatory environment, facilities, and equipment.  
   * Management section – specify the business structure, ownership percentages, key personnel, and who will manage day‑to‑day operations and long‑term strategy. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)  
   * Market section – identify target customers, estimate market size, analyze competitors, and outline marketing tactics. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)  
   * Money section – include the following financial documents:  
     * Sources and uses of funds statement  
     * Three‑year income projection (monthly for each of the next 36 months)  
     * Three‑year cash‑flow projection  
     * Balance sheet snapshot  
     * Break‑even analysis [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  

2. **Gather and organize supporting information.**  
   * Research industry statistics and growth prospects (use any available market data).  
   * Draft product/service descriptions, including development stage, testing, and quality assurance.  
   * List required licenses, permits, and ongoing regulatory obligations [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).  

3. **Create a presentable document.**  
   * Include a table of contents (optional).  
   * Attach relevant documents as exhibits: resumes, legal filings, contracts, floor plans, etc. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13).  
   * Keep the plan concise yet comprehensive—most readers skim the executive summary first, so make it compelling.  

**How to set up accounting for a new small business (based on IRS Publication 583 & Publication 334)**  

1. **Choose a tax year.**  
   * You can adopt a calendar tax year (Jan 1 – Dec 31) or a fiscal tax year (12 consecutive months ending on any month‑except Dec). The choice is made when you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

2. **Select an accounting method.**  
   * **Cash method** – record income when received and expenses when paid. It is common for sole proprietors without inventory.  
   * **Accrual method** – record income when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash flow. Required if you maintain inventory.  
   * A **combination method** may be used if it clearly shows income and you keep separate books for each set of items. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

3. **Maintain proper books and records.**  
   * Keep complete and separate records for each business.  
   * If you choose the cash method, you may still account for inventory as non‑incidental supplies; otherwise you must use the accrual method for inventory. Small‑business taxpayers are exempt from the inventory rule if you treat inventory as non‑incidental. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=45)  

4. **File the required forms.**  
   * **Schedule C (Form 1040)** – reports business income and expenses.  
   * **Schedule SE (Form 1040)** – calculates self‑employment tax.  
   * **Form 1128** – if you later need to change the tax year or accounting method, IRS approval is required. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

5. **Keep tax‑related records.**  
   * Retain receipts, invoices, and bank statements that support all deductibles.  
   * Separate personal and business expenses; only ordinary and necessary business expenses are deductible. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=32)  

By following the SBA outline you’ll have a professional‑looking business plan, and by setting up your accounting with the IRS‑recommended method and bookkeeping practices you’ll be ready for accurate tax reporting and financial management.

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do you need an EIN?**  
Yes, if you are operating a business that is a partnership, corporation, or LLC, or if you are a sole proprietor who wants a separate business identity, you must obtain an EIN.  Additionally, you must get an EIN if you:  

- Pay wages to one or more employees, or  
- File pension or excise tax returns.  

> “EINs are assigned to sole proprietors, LLCs, corporations, and partnerships for tax filing and reporting purposes. … If you have employees, you must also have an EIN to use as a TIN if you do either of the following… Pay wages to one or more employees. File pension or excise tax returns.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

If you are a sole proprietor without employees, you can use your Social Security number as your TIN, but obtaining an EIN is still recommended if you want a distinct business number.

**What accounting method does the EIN come with?**  
The EIN itself does not dictate an accounting method.  When you file your first income‑tax return, you select an accounting method for the business.  The IRS publication outlines the available options:  

- **Cash method:** report income when received and expenses when paid.  
- **Accrual method:** report income when earned and expenses when incurred, even if the payment occurs later.  

> “An accounting method is a set of rules used to determine when and how income and expenses are reported. You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return. There are two basic accounting methods. 1. Cash method. 2. Accrual method.”  
> [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

If your business keeps inventory, you generally must use the accrual method for inventory purchases and sales (unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer with a special rule).  Thus, the EIN does **not** determine the accounting method; you decide that independently during your first tax return filing.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 6)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them
results.answer:
The handbook requires that all **recordable** work‑related injuries and illnesses be logged on:

* **OSHA Form 300** – the Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses  
* **OSHA Form 301** – the Injury and Illness Incident Report (a supplementary record for each log entry)  
* **OSHA Form 300A** – the Summary of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses (prepared annually)  

These records must be kept at the worksite for **at least five years** (the handbook does not specify a shorter period) – for example, “Injury and illness records (OSHA 300, 300A, and 301) are kept at the worksite for at least five years.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) 

The handbook also notes that occupation injuries or illnesses, except minor first‑aid‑only incidents, are recorded on the OSHA 300 and that the supplementary 301 reports must also be retained [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

results.question: how do i register a trademark
results.answer:
To register a trademark, you can file with either a state‑level office or the federal U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).  

1. **Choose the level of registration** – decide whether to register the mark in the state where your business operates or to seek federal registration through the USPTO.  
2. **Search existing marks** – before filing, use the online trademark databases to make sure your chosen name has not already been taken.  
3. **File the application**  
   * **State registration** – file with the Secretary of State.  
   * **Federal registration** – file with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.  

4. **Contact information**  
   * Secretary of State – (605) 773‑2797, https://sdsos.gov/  
   * USPTO – (703) 308‑HELP or (800) 786‑9199, www.uspto.gov  

These steps are outlined in the South Dakota Business Planning Guide:
